# `ggbreak`: set axis breaks for 'ggplot2'


[![CRAN_Status_Badge](http://www.r-pkg.org/badges/version/ggbreak?color=green)](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ggbreak)
![](http://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/grand-total/ggbreak?color=green)
![](http://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/ggbreak?color=green)
![](http://cranlogs.r-pkg.org/badges/last-week/ggbreak?color=green)



```{r comment="", echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat(read.dcf("DESCRIPTION", fields = "Description")[1, 1])
```



## :bulb: Overview

Some datasets are not normally distributed and hold outliers that are
meaningful.  A bar plot of one of them is a few readable bars and one that
is a thousand times taller: the bulk of the data is flattened into a line at
the bottom of the panel and the reader learns nothing from it.  A
logarithmic axis is the usual answer, and it is the right one when the data
is log-normal, but it cannot be used when the values include zero or
negative ones, and even where it can be used it changes what the reader
sees -- equal ratios become equal distances, and the outliers stop looking
like outliers.

`ggbreak` takes the other way out.  It keeps the scale the data is on and
makes the *axis* discontinuous: a range that holds no interesting value is
hidden, and the rest of the axis is drawn in separate panels that sit next
to each other with a small gap between them.  The bulk of the data is then
drawn at a size that can be read, and the outliers are still there, at the
end of the axis, with the gap telling the reader that the axis does not run
straight.

The scale functions are ordinary `ggplot2` scales, so `+` keeps working
after one of them is added: a broken plot is still a `gg` plot that more
layers can be added to, and it takes the same themes, labels, legends,
`coord_flip()` and scale transformations as any other.  A plot can be broken
on the x axis and on the y axis at the same time, and that is the only
combination that is allowed -- a break, a cut and a wrap cannot be mixed,
and a plot that asks for two of them says which two it was given instead of
drawing something wrong.

### Clipping, not cutting

A break is drawn by **clipping**.  Every panel is given the whole dataset and
hides the part of it that belongs to the other panels, rather than the data
being divided between them.  Two consequences are worth knowing.  A point or
a line that crosses the break is drawn into both of the panels that meet
there, so a trend that runs across the break keeps the piece that joins it
up, and a line can be bridged across the gap with `bridge = TRUE`.  And what
a panel hides is not written to the file, so a PDF or an SVG written from a
broken plot holds no object larger than the figure and can be pasted into
Adobe Illustrator -- before 0.2.0 a bar reaching from 0 to 990 was written
out at its full height in the panel that shows its top.

## :sparkles: Features

Five scales, for the three ways of bringing a long axis under control:

| Function | What it draws |
| --- | --- |
| `scale_x_break()`, `scale_y_break()` | a **gap plot** |
| `scale_x_cut()`, `scale_y_cut()` | a **cut plot** |
| `scale_wrap(n = )` | a **wrap plot** |

A **gap plot** hides a range of the axis and draws what is left in panels
next to each other, with a gap between them.  A **cut plot** cuts the axis
into slices at the given points, and the points are the boundaries of the
slices, so the data next to a boundary is kept in both of the slices that
meet there and a trend can be followed across it; `which` selects the slices
to resize and `scales` says by how much.  A **wrap plot** keeps the whole
axis and splits it into `n` consecutive windows of the same width, one per
row, so a long series becomes readable without dropping anything from it.

Between them the scales also support:

- **any number of break points** on an axis, and a break on each axis at
  once;
- **a discrete axis**, and **a date or datetime axis**;
- **`space`**, the gap between the panels, in centimetres;
- **`symbol = "slash"`**, which marks the break on the axis;
- **`ticklabels`**, the tick labels of the panels;
- **`scales`**, the relative size of the panels: `"fixed"` (the default)
  gives each panel a share proportional to the range it covers, `"free"`
  gives them equal shares, and a number is a multiple of the first panel;
- **`bridge = TRUE`**, which joins up a line that crosses a break, so a
  connected scatter plot reads as one line instead of two.

A broken plot works with:

- `facet_grid()` and `facet_wrap()`;
- `coord_flip()`, reverse scales and scale transformations;
- secondary axes;
- legends, and every label of the plot;
- `ggrepel`;
- a `patchwork`, `cowplot` or `gridExtra` layout.

## :arrow_double_down: Installation

Get the released version from CRAN:

```r
install.packages("ggbreak")
```


Or the development version from github:

```r
## install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("YuLab-SMU/ggbreak")
```

## :books: Documentation

- The [vignette](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggbreak/vignettes/ggbreak.html)
  works through the scales and what each of them can do, with a figure for
  every feature.  It opens with the
  [introduction](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggbreak/vignettes/ggbreak.html#introduction)
  and closes with a [FAQ](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggbreak/vignettes/ggbreak.html#faq)
  of the questions that come up most often.
- The help pages of the scales: `?scale_x_break`, `?scale_x_cut`,
  `?scale_wrap`.
- The [issues](https://github.com/YuLab-SMU/ggbreak/issues) are the place to
  ask about anything the vignette does not answer.
